name: llm-d
notable_features: CNCF sandbox project founded by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave and NVIDIA - deliberately vendor-neutral where Dynamo is NVIDIA-originated
Same layering as Dynamo: orchestration and optimisation ABOVE vLLM and SGLang, which 'handle efficiently running large language models on accelerators'
Intelligent routing: prefix-cache- and load-aware balancing, plus experimental predicted-latency-based scheduling
Advanced KV-cache management: 'tiered offloading to CPU or disk and precise global indexing of the KV cache state' to increase the effective working set for multi-turn requests
PD disaggregation combined with wide expert parallelism for very large models (DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS class)
SLO-aware autoscaling from live inference signals, intelligent flow control for multi-tenancy, and OpenAI-compatible Batch APIs
Well-lit-path guides with benchmarked recipes and Helm charts, plus accelerator/network/configuration matrices
hardware_caveats: Kubernetes is the deployment substrate; the differentiator is Helm/operator work, so a bare-metal shop gains less
Vendor-neutral in governance, but the tested recipes and partner benchmarks are NVIDIA- and AMD-centric; other accelerators are 'points of contact' rather than benchmarked paths
Prefix-cache-aware routing only pays if replicas actually share prefixes - without a shared KV index the routing decision is guesswork
best_for: Kubernetes production serving where PD disaggregation and tiered KV need to be operated rather than hand-rolled
Shops that want disaggregation without betting on a single vendor's stack, given the CNCF governance and multi-vendor founding
Multi-turn or long-context workloads where the effective KV working set exceeds per-replica HBM
avoid_for: Non-Kubernetes deployments - the value is in the operator, planner and guides
Single-node serving, where none of the four themes apply
Workloads with no prefix locality, where prefix-cache-aware routing adds a hop for no reuse
notes: KV transfer path: llm-d does not define its own transport - it composes the engines' connectors (NIXL/UCX, Mooncake) for the PD handoff and implements its own GPU->CPU/disk tiering with a global KV index. Partner-reported performance claims in the README, attributed as such: 'Up to 70% higher tokens/sec with prefill/decode disaggregation vs standard vLLM - GPT-OSS on NVIDIA B200 (p6-b200), AWS'; '10-30% throughput improvement with disaggregated serving on identical infrastructure - GPT-OSS-120B and Llama 3.3 70B on AMD MI300X, Oracle'; '3x higher output throughput and 2x faster TTFT with prefix-cache-aware routing vs round-robin - Llama 3.1 70B on 4x AMD MI300X, Tesla / Red Hat'; '40% reduction in TTFT and ITL with predicted-latency scheduling vs heuristics on NVIDIA GPUs, Google'. These are vendor blog figures, not independent measurements, and the PD number is a throughput comparison that vLLM's own docs would call into question ('Disaggregated prefill DOES NOT improve throughput' - a claim about a fixed-SLO single-node setup, so the two are not measuring the same thing). Recorded as a production system, not a paper, but with the caveat that most of its published numbers come from partners.
